Molecules split and atoms rejoin — what decides which way a reacting mixture moves?

About: the Gibbs function against extent of reaction for A₂ ⇌ 2A

Source

Concept
The Gibbs function G of an ideal-gas mixture undergoing A₂ ⇌ 2A at fixed temperature T and total pressure p = p₀, drawn against the extent of reaction ξ (ξ = 0 pure A₂, ξ = 1 complete dissociation; at extent ξ the vessel holds N₀(1 − ξ) molecules and 2N₀ξ atoms). The orange tangent has slope Σᵢ νᵢμᵢ, which the strip below plots divided by kBT.
Serves
Explaining what decides whether a reacting mixture at fixed T and p runs forwards or backwards, and where it comes to rest from different starting compositions.
Inquiry
Five questions, each answered before checking in the sim: releases from ξ = 0.02 and ξ = 0.90 at Δφ/kBT = +1 and from ξ = 0.98 at −2, a comparison of the readouts Q and K at rest, and a test of which combination of Q and K gives the slope. A closing card states the rule: Q < K runs forwards, Q > K backwards.
Misconception
The options in each question are common intuitions about what sets the direction and the end point of a reaction; each is addressed by feedback only after the student commits.
On screen
Δφ/kBT (−2 to +2, steps of 0.5) sets the standard Gibbs change per reaction event and K = e−Δφ/kBT. The starting-extent slider, its number box, or a drag on the graph places the marker in steps of 0.01; Release lets the mixture move from there. The marker's speed is for display only. When a release ends, a dot with dashed guides marks the minimum of the curve, labelled ξₑ; the guides clear when the marker or Δφ/kBT is changed. A small vessel view in the upper left shows the mixture at the marker: 20 A₂ molecules to start, with each dissociated molecule drawn as two free A atoms.
Scales
The G axis is unnumbered and fixed over g = (G − N₀μ⁰A₂)/(N₀kBT) from −2.5 to +2.5; the bracket at ξ = 1 marks the height N₀Δφ between the two ends of the curve. The strip is fixed from −6 to +6. The Readouts panel, below the controls: ξ and Σᵢ νᵢμᵢ/kBT to 3 decimal places; Q = (pA/p₀)²/(pA₂/p₀) = 4ξ²/(1 − ξ²) for the present mixture and K, both to 3 significant figures.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit, then checkEach of the five questions is answered before Next; the minimum of G stays unmarked until a release has ended, and the Q readout appears only from the question that uses it.
Cognitive conflictEvery option carries the expert explanation, tied to readouts the student can check on screen at the same setting.
Operational quantitiesξ, Σᵢ νᵢμᵢ/kBT, Q and K are shown to the precision the questions quote; the slope appears three ways — the tangent, the strip and the readout.
What stays fixedK depends only on Δφ/kBT and does not change as the marker moves; Q changes with the composition.
Stable scalesThe G axis is fixed over g from −2.5 to +2.5 and the strip over −6 to +6, so a change of Δφ/kBT visibly reshapes both curves.
Honest animationThe marker's speed is labelled as display-only; thermodynamics fixes the direction and end point of a change, not its rate.
Which Way a Reaction Runs
Gibbs function against extent of reaction G(ξ) · A₂ ⇌ 2A · T fixed · p = p₀
Slope of G along ξ: Σᵢ νᵢμᵢ / kBT

Guided Inquiry

1 · Starting from almost pure A₂

Set Δφ/kBT to +1, so K reads 0.368 and the standard change is unfavourable. Put the marker at ξ = 0.02 (type it in the box), where the tangent slopes downwards and Σᵢνᵢμᵢ/kBT reads −5.437, and press Release. What does the mixture do?

2 · Starting from mostly atoms

Keep Δφ/kBT = +1. Put the marker at ξ = 0.90, a mixture made mostly of atoms, and press Release. Where does the mixture come to rest?

3 · A favourable standard change

Set Δφ/kBT to −2, so K reads 7.39 and the standard change now favours the atoms. Put the marker at ξ = 0.98, almost complete dissociation, and press Release. What does the mixture do?

4 · Q and K at rest

Keep Δφ/kBT = −2 and let the mixture come to rest from any start, then compare the readouts Q and K. Repeat at Δφ/kBT = +1 and at 0. When the mixture is at rest, how is Q related to K?

5 · What sets the slope

Set Δφ/kBT to +1 and put the marker at ξ = 0.50, without releasing it. The readouts give Σᵢνᵢμᵢ/kBT = +1.288, Q = 1.33 and K = 0.368. Which combination of Q and K gives the slope?

6 · What this shows

At fixed T and p a reacting mixture moves downhill in G. The slope, Σᵢνᵢμᵢ = kBT ln(Q/K), decides the direction: Q < K runs forwards, Q > K runs backwards.

It comes to rest at the minimum of G, where Q = K, from either side. Δφ fixes K, and so where the minimum lies, but never the direction on its own.

Q is the product ∏ᵢ(pᵢ/p₀)νᵢ of the notes' law of mass action, taken at the marker rather than at rest: with μᵢ = μ⁰ᵢ + kBT ln(pᵢ/p₀), the slope is Σᵢνᵢμᵢ = Δφ + kBT ln Q = kBT ln(Q/K), which vanishes exactly when Q = K.

Which Way a Reaction Runs

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A gas of A2 molecules and A atoms, held at fixed temperature T and total pressure p = p0, can turn molecules into atoms or atoms back into molecules. This sim plots the Gibbs function G of that mixture against how far the reaction A2 ⇌ 2A has gone, and lets you release a mixture from any composition.

What you'll learn

  • How the extent ξ counts the reaction.
  • What the slope of G against ξ is, in terms of the chemical potentials.
  • How that slope is built from Δφ, K and the mixture.
  • Where a released mixture comes to rest, and how you can tell beforehand.
The set-up: one vessel, two ends of the reaction, T and p held fixed.

What's on screen

  • Blue curve: G against ξ, per N0 and in units of kBT, from ξ = 0 (all A2) to ξ = 1 (all A). The axis has no numbers.
  • Orange marker and tangent: the marker sits at the present ξ, and the tangent's slope is Σiνiμi.
  • Vessel view (upper left): grey molecules and green atoms for the mixture at the marker.
  • Strip (below the graph): the slope in units of kBT, from −6 to +6.
  • Readouts: ξ, the slope, Q and K.
See itStart the sim again at your own settings. Watch for: the blue curve with the orange marker and tangent, and the readouts for your Δφ and ξ.

03

The extent ξ counts the reaction

The notes write the reaction as ΣiνiXi = 0 (3.61). For A2 ⇌ 2A that is 2A − A2 = 0, so νA = 2 and νA2 = −1. When the reaction advances by dξ, the numbers change by dNi = νi dξ (3.62): two atoms appear for each molecule lost.

The sim scales ξ as in the notes' Figure 23: ξ = 0 is pure A2 and ξ = 1 is complete dissociation. Then A2 has N0(1 − ξ) molecules and A has 2N0ξ atoms.

Numbers present against ξ. With N0 = 20, ξ = 0.50 is 10 molecules and 20 atoms.

G of the mixture depends on ξ at fixed T and p. A small advance dξ changes G by Σiμi dNi (3.63), so the slope of G is the sum below. The orange tangent has this slope.

Notes (3.62) and (3.64). The strip plots this slope divided by kBT.
See itPut the marker at ξ = 0.50. Watch for: the vessel view with 10 molecules and 20 atoms, and ξ reading 0.500.
04

The slope of G is kBT ln(Q/K)

For ideal gases each species has μi = μ0i(T) + kBT ln(pi/p0) (3.66). Put this into the slope. With Δφ = Σiνiμ0i, the reaction quotient Q = Πi(pi/p0)νi and the equilibrium constant K = e−Δφ/kBT (3.69), the slope is:

The sim shows this in the strip and in the slope readout.

The partial pressures are pA = 2ξp/(1 + ξ) and pA2 = (1 − ξ)p/(1 + ξ), as in (3.72), so at p = p0 the quotient depends on ξ alone.

Q for this stoichiometry. The sim prints it as the readout Q.

Δφ fixes K once and for all. The mixture fixes Q. At Δφ/kBT = +1, K = 0.368. At ξ = 0.10, Q = 0.0404 and the slope is ln(0.0404/0.368) = −2.209. A negative slope means G falls as ξ grows, so the reaction runs forward. A positive slope means it runs backward (notes, after 3.65).

See itPut the marker at ξ = 0.10 with Δφ/kBT = +1. Watch for: the tangent sloping downward, with the slope readout at −2.209, Q at 0.0404 and K at 0.368.
05

A mixture rests where Q equals K

The mixture moves downhill in G and rests where the slope vanishes, Σiνiμi = 0 (3.65). With the slope kBT ln(Q/K), that is Q = K, the law of mass action.

Q grows steadily with ξ, from 0 at ξ = 0 to ∞ at ξ = 1, so Q = K happens at one ξ only. Solving 4ξ2/(1 − ξ2) = K gives the notes' (3.75) at p = p0, with α written as ξ.

The minimum of G, as a function of K alone.
G against ξ at Δφ/kBT = +1. Each tangent points downhill toward the same minimum.

At +1, K = 0.368 and ξe = 0.290. Released at ξ = 0.02, Q = 1.60×10−3 is below K and the slope is −5.437, so the marker runs right and stops at 0.290. Released at ξ = 0.90, Q = 17.1 is above K and the slope is +3.836, so it runs left to the same 0.290. The slope is −∞ at ξ = 0 and +∞ at ξ = 1 (notes, Figure 23), so the minimum is always inside.

See itRelease the mixture from ξ = 0.02 at Δφ/kBT = +1. Watch for: the marker running right and stopping at ξ = 0.290 in about 6 s, with Q reaching K = 0.368 and the slope reaching 0.
06

The side you start on sets the direction

Δφ fixes K, so it fixes where the minimum lies. It does not say which side of the minimum you start on, and the slope at the marker depends on that side. Q < K runs forward. Q > K runs backward.

Take Δφ/kBT = −2, which favours the atoms. Then K = 7.39 and ξe = 0.805. Release the marker at ξ = 0.98. Here Q = 97.0, and ln(Q/K) = +2.575. The slope is positive even though Δφ is negative.

G against ξ at Δφ/kBT = −2. The marker at 0.98 is on the uphill side of the minimum.

So the marker runs backward, atoms recombining, and stops at 0.805. The standard change favours atoms, but a mixture already richer in atoms than the minimum has too many of them. The rule is the same as before: the sign of ln(Q/K) decides.

See itRelease from ξ = 0.98 at Δφ/kBT = −2. Watch for: the marker running left and stopping at ξ = 0.805 in about 6 s, the slope readout starting at +2.575.
07

Δφ moves the minimum, not the rule

Raising Δφ/kBT lowers K, and ξe = (1 + 4/K)−1/2 falls with it. Across the slider, ξe reads 0.805 at −2, 0.447 at 0, 0.290 at +1 and 0.181 at +2.

The resting extent ξe against Δφ/kBT, for p = p0.

At Δφ = 0, K = 1 and the minimum sits where Q = 1, that is at ξ = 1/√5 = 0.447. At 0.447 the vessel view shows 11 molecules and 18 atoms. At no setting does ξe reach 0 or 1, because each end of the curve is infinitely steep.

See itRelease from ξ = 0.02 at Δφ = 0. Watch for: the marker stopping at ξ = 0.447, with Q and K both reading 1.00, in about 8 s.
08

Where it matters

  • Law of mass action. At rest, Πi(pi/p0)νi = K(T). The value of K depends on temperature and nothing else (notes, §3.4). Pressure and composition enter only through the partial pressures.
  • The notes' example. Dissociation of a diatomic gas, A2 ⇌ 2A, is worked in (3.72) to (3.75). The degree of dissociation α is the sim's ξ at p = p0, and at other pressures a factor p/p0 multiplies Q. The sim holds p = p0.
  • Temperature. K(T) changes with temperature by the van ’t Hoff relation (3.71). The sim holds T fixed: each Δφ/kBT setting is one reaction at one temperature.
  • Direction, not rate. The sim shows which way a mixture goes and where it stops. The marker speed is a display choice, and the sim has no model of how fast a real reaction proceeds.
09

Summary

In one line. The slope of G against ξ is built from a standard change Δφ and a term for the mixture, and the sim lets you release a mixture to see what the two decide together.

Key points

  • dNi = νi dξ, so the slope of G is Σiνiμi, which equals kBT ln(Q/K).
  • Q < K runs forward and Q > K runs backward. A mixture rests where Q = K.
  • At p = p0, ξe = (1 + 4/K)−1/2 with K = e−Δφ/kBT.

Common mix-ups

  • “Δφ < 0 means the reaction runs forward from anywhere.” At Δφ/kBT = −2, a mixture at ξ = 0.98 runs back to 0.805.
  • “The slope is Δφ.” The slope is kBT ln(Q/K). At the opening it reads −5.437, not +1.
  • “Equilibrium means ξ = 0 or ξ = 1.” It is the minimum in between. At Δφ = 0 it is at 0.447.
  • “Q and K are the same number.” They match only at rest. Elsewhere their ratio sets the slope.

Things to try on your own

  • At Δφ/kBT = +1, release from ξ = 0.10, 0.50 and 0.90, and compare where they stop.
  • Step Δφ/kBT from −2 to +2 and read ξe each time.
  • At any setting, set the marker near the minimum and compare Q with K.
